CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK
  AND THE CITY COUNCIL ACTING ON BEHALF OF THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY

  AGENDA

  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING

  Wednesday
  December 16, 2020
  6:30 p.m.

  EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. N-29-20
  These meetings will be conducted pursuant to Section 3 of Executive Order No. N-29-
  20 issued by Governor Newsom on March 17, 2020.

  Accordingly, Councilmembers will be provided with a meeting login number and
  conference call number; they will not be physically present at Council Chambers.

  Pursuant to the Governor’s order, the public may provide public comment utilizing the
  methods set forth below.

  Note that City Hall is currently closed to the public. You will not be admitted to City Hall.

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.

This Agenda may include items considered by the City Council acting on behalf of the Successor Agency
of the former Monterey Park Redevelopment Agency which dissolved February 1, 2012. Successor
Agency matters will include the notation of “SA” next to the Agenda Item Number.

  Page 1 of 322

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
In accordance with Executive Order No. N-29-20 and guidance from the California Department of Public
Health on gatherings, remote public participation is allowed in the following ways:

Via Email
Public comment will be accepted up to 24 hours before the meeting via email to
mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov and, when feasible, read into the record during public comment. Written
communications are limited to not more than 50 words.

Via Telephone
Public comment may be submitted via telephone during the meeting, before the close of public comment,
by calling (888) 788-0099 or (877) 853-5247 and entering Zoom Meeting ID: 995 9335 7089 then press
pound (#). When prompted to enter participation ID number press pound (#) again. If participants would
like to make a public comment they will enter “*9” then the Clerk’s office will be notified, and you will be
in the rotation to make a public comment. Press “*6” to unmute yourself when called upon to speak.
Participants are encouraged to join the meeting 15 minutes before the start of the meeting. You may
speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. Speakers will not be allowed to combine time. The Mayor and
City Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. As part of the virtual meeting
protocols, anonymous persons will not be allowed to provide public comment.

Important Disclaimer
When a participant calls in to join the meeting, their name and/or phone number will be visible to all
participants. Note that all public meetings will be recorded.

November 25,2020, LAIF's interest rate is .51o/o. Conversely, CaIPERS current OPEB

 SUBJECT:  Pension Obligation Bond Update

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing the Pension Obligation Bond Update; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On October 7,2020 staff provided the City Council with a financing update for the City's
pending Pension Obligation Bonds (POB) issuance. At that time, based on a legal review
by the City's bond counsel of the validation process completed by the City in 2004, the
City was not required to validate the proposed issuance of additional POBs. At the time,
staff and the City's financial advisor estimate the three month acceleration of the schedule
could save the City an additional $1,030,533.

Since the prior update, staff has been working with the financing team to prepare legal
and bond financing documents. To ensure the Preliminary Official Statement (POS) and
Official Statement (OS) contain current financial data, the schedule has been slightly
modified to allow for the City's Fiscal Year 2019-20 Comprehensive Annual Financial
Report (CAFR) to be completed. This will provide the most recent information to investors
and maximize savings by helping secure the lowest interest rate possible. The POS and
supporting financing documents are scheduled for presentation to the City Council on
January 20,2021. Based on the schedule below, staff and the financing team estimate
the City will enter the market on February 2, 2021 and close the transaction by mid-
February 2021.

BACKGROUND:

As of the June 30,2019 actuarialvaluation, the City had a total Unfunded Accrued Liability
(UAL) of $108,647,509, comprised of approximately $43.3 million for Miscellaneous
employees and approximately $65.3 million for Safety employees. UFI and City staff will
continue to work together to evaluate the most efficient and beneficial approach to
refinance all or a portion of the City's UAL through issuance of the POBs.

interest cost (TlC) for the Bonds. Other documents include a Bond Purchase Agreement,

1  DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY: ELECTION-RELATED CIVIL UNREST (THIS
  ITEM IS ANTICIPATED TO BE CONTINUED TO THE REGULAR MEETING
  STARTING AT 6:30 P.M.)

  Following May 25, 2020, protests throughout Los Angeles County resulted in
  widespread arson, looting, assaults, vandalism and rioting. Days later, the
  Governor issued a Proclamation of Emergency for Los Angeles County, and the
  County of Los Angeles Board of Supervisors imposed a curfew for the protection of
  public order and safety. Events similar to those of May 25, 2020, have lead to
  further civil unrest in cities across the nation, which continue to this day.

  This widespread civil unrest across the nation has carried over to general acrimony
  surrounding the 2020 general election to be held on November 3, 2020. The rise of
  domestic groups with extremist ideologies, combined with the continuing turmoil

  due to dilapidated conditions. Staff has been working toward obtaining the

  have been replaced over the years to keep the pool in operation, the entire facility
  needs to be renovated to meet current ADA standards and a pool recirculation
  system needs to be installed to recycle water.

  grant provides an opportunity for the City to apply for grant funds to design,

 SUBJEGT:  Professional Services Amendments for Community Development Block
  Grant and Home lnvestment Partnerships Program Services

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute an amendment, in a form approved by
  the City Attorney, to an agreement with Priscila Davila & Associates for an amount
  of $100,000 and an agreement with HP Housing Programs for an amount of
  $260,000, both for a 3-year term; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

ln 2016, the City circulated a RFP to at least 17 professional consulting firms to provide
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and Home lmprovement lnvestment
Partnerships Program (HOME) administration services to the City of Monterey Park. Of
the 17 firms, 5 responded. On January 18,2017 , City Council authorized the City Manager
to enter into a 3-year professional services agreement with both Priscila Davila &
Associates and HP Housing Programs. The City is requested authorizing the City
Manager to enter into a second 3-year term with both Priscila Davila & Associates for an
amount of $100,000 and HP Housing Programs for an amount of $260,000.

BACKGROUND:

Every year the City of Monterey Park receives CDBG and HOME funds from the United
States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Under this federal
program, the City is obligated to spend HOME funds exclusively to create affordable
housing for low-income households or rehabilitate existing residential dwelling unit whose
owner meets specific income requirements. CDBG funds allow for more flexible spending
that address a wide range of unique community development needs with the
understanding that the City is ultimately meeting a national objective(s) that expand
economic opportunities and fulfill community needs that benefit low to moderate-income
households.

Due to the complexity of federal regulations, COVID 19 impacts and the continuity of
services during these difficult times, staff is recommending that City Council authorize the
amendment to extend the Priscila Davila & Associates Agreement to provide CDBG and
Home administrative services for an amount of $100,000 for a term of February 1, 2021
to June 30,2024, and HP Housing Programs Agreement to manage the City's Housing
Rehabilitation Program and monitor the affordable housing assets in the community for
an amount of $260,000 for a term of February 1,2021 to June 30,2024.

FISCAL IMPACT:

No General Fund revenue will be used to fund the programs or consulting service
provided as part of these contracts. Funding to pay the contracts will come specifically
from CDBG, HOME and Housing funds as identified in the City's annual budget and the
AnnualAction Plan.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Adopting the Resolution approving the State mandated minimum wage increase
  in order to have the wage adjustments in place as of January 1,2021; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Effective January 1, 2021, California's Minimum Wage for employers with 26 or more
employees will be increasing from $13.00 an hour to $14.00 an hour. The minimum
wage increase will impact ten (10) positions that are below the mandated increase as
follows:

  . Cashier
  o Junior Lifeguard
  . Library Page
  . Locker Room Attendant
  o School Crossing Guard
  o Recreation Leader
  . Fire lntern I

  . Lifeguard
  . Community Media Specialist
  o Planning lntern
The minimum wage increase applied to the above positions will impact the wage gap
between the classifications of Lifeguard and Senior Lifeguard. ln order to maintain an
appropriate wage gap between these classifications, the salary range for Senior
Lifeguard will be adjusted in conjunction with these minimum wage increases.

ln order to have the State mandated minimum wage increase adjustments in place by
January 1, 2021, staff is requesting that the City Council approve the attached
resolution.

BACKGROUND:

On September 25,2013, the California Legislature adopted AB 10 which amends Labor
Code Section 1182.12 to increase the California minimum wage to $15.00 an hour by
the year 2022. Effective July 1 , 2014, the minimum wage was increased to $9.00 per
hour with $0.50 cent increases in January 2015, January 2016, and January 2017.
Beginning January 2018, the minimum wage increased by $t.00 per hour to $1 1.00 with
$1.00 per hour increase for January 1,2019 and January 2020. The final increase will
occur on January 1, 2022, with the minimum wage increases reaching $15.00 per hour.

The City currently has eleven (11) part-time classifications whose hourly wage falls
below the mandated $14.00 an hour state mandated increase. This state mandated
wage increase will also impact the wage gap of one (1) higher level parttime
classification. ln order to keep the consistency and difference in pay between the part-
time classifications of Lifeguard and Senior Lifeguard, the salary range for the higher-
level classification of Senior Lifeguard will be adjusted to maintain an appropriate wage
gap.

FISCAL IMPAGT:
All part time staff are currently at zero hours, therefore there is no fiscal impact for the
remainder o12020-2021 FY (January 2021 - June 2021).

economic relations between the parties to provide an orderly and peaceful means of resolving any
misunderstandings or differences which may arise, and to set forth the basic and full agreement
between the parties concerning wages, hours of employment, and other conditions of employment.
Unless otherwise noted, all provisions of the MOU become effective the beginning of the pay
period following City Council approval of the MOU.

  ARTICLE 7: GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE

 Except as modified herein, the Grievance Procedure shall be governed by Personnel Rule XV,
 Disciplinary Proceedings, Sec. 6, Grievances. ofthe Personnel Rules and Regulations ofthe City
 of Monterey Park which is outlined as follows:

 The presentation and hearing of all employee grievances shall be governed by the following rules

A  A grievance shall be defined as an alleged violation of a specific provision of this
  Memorandum of Understanding, the City Personnel Rules and Regulations, or of the Rules
  and Regulations validly propagated by any department within the City, or State Law
  governing conditions of employment. The grievance procedure shall not be utilized by an
  employee to contest the content of a performance evaluation, verbal or written reprimands
  or other documentation regarding the employee's work perfoffnance yet which is not
  defined as "disciplinary action" by Rule XV of the City Personnel Rules and Regulations.

  Discipline shall be imposed in such a manner as to not violate the FLSA with regard to
  "exempt" employees.

B  All grievances shall be filed in writing with the immediate supervisor of the person
  aggrieved within fifteen (15) calendar days after the employee knows, or in the exercise of
  reasonable diligence, would have known, of the occulrence in question.

C.  Written notice of disposition of the grievance shall be filed with the next higher
  administrative authority by the supervisor with whom the grievance was originally filed.
  Such notice shall be filed within fifteen (15) calendar days of the original filing of the
  grievance.

 D  If satisfactory redress is not obtained by the employee from the immediate supervisor,
  the grievance may be appealed in writing through the normal administrative organtzation: that
  is, first to the Division Manager; second, the Department Director and third, the City Manager.
  In each case a written notice of disposition must be forwarded to the gnevant and to the next
  higher authority within fifteen (15) calendar days of receipt of the employee's written
  grievance.

E.  The City Manager shall be the final authority in all cases except those in which a
  violation of the Personnel Ordinance or Rules is alleged. The City Manager shall forward
  notice of disposition of such grievance to the grievant within fifteen (15) calendar days of
  receipt of the employee's written grievance.

F  In the case of those grievances in which a violation of the Personnel Ordinance or
  Rules is alleged, an employee may appeal to the Personnel Board after the procedures set
  forth above have been exhausted.

  Such appeals will be filed in writing with the Director of Human Resources and Risk
  Management who will cause them to be brought to the attention ofthe Board. The Board will
  review such appeals and determine whether an investigation and/or hearing should be held.
  This preliminary consideration of an appeal will not constitute a hearing by the Board. Within
  ten (10) calendar days after concluding a hearing pursuant to this section, the Personnel
  Board shall certif,i its findings and decision in writing to the City Council, to the City
  Manager, and to any other official from whose action the appeal is taken, and to the affected
  employee.

  Recommendations by the Board for redress of grievances will be addressed to the City
  Manager and shall be advisory in nature.

leave, or accumulated compensatory time off While Temporarily Totally Disabled (TTD), the

wage or salary.

instances where the employee is either permanent, stationary and incapacitated for the perfofinance

employee, although not permanent and stationary, will recover to the extent necessary to perform
the essential duties of his/her position regardless of whether or not any form of paid leave remains
in the employee's various paid leave accounts.

accrue all fringe benefits.

Nothing herein shall prohibit an employee from requesting a leave of absence without pay from
the City Council. Such leave is not guaranteed, nor may it exceed beyond a period of one (1) year
from date of injury.

A.  Policy and Standards for Determination of Appropriate Units

 The policy objectives in determining the appropriateness of units shall include: (l)
efficient operations of the City and its compatibility with the primary responsibility of
the City and its employees to effectively and economically serve the public, and on (2)
providing employees with effective representation based on recognized community of
interest considerations. These policy objectives require that the appropriate unit shall be
the broadest feasible grouping of positions that share an identifiable community of
interest. Factors to be considered shall be:

1  Similarity of the general kinds of work performed, types of qualifications required,
  and the general working conditions.

2  History of representation in the City and in similar employment; except however,
  that no unit shall be deemed to be an appropriate unit solely on the basis of the
  extent to which employees in the proposed unit have organized.

3.  Consistency with the organizational patterns of the City.

4.  Number of employees and classifications, and the effect on the administration of
  employer-employee relations because of the fragmentation of classifications and/or
  proliferation of units.

5  Effect on the classification structure and impact on the stability of the employer-
  employee relationship because of dividing a single or related classification among
  two or more units.

Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions of this Section, managerial, supervisory and
confidential responsibilities, as defined in this Section, are determinative factors in
establishing appropriate units hereunder. Therefore, such managerial, supelisory and

  ARTICLE 7: GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE

Except as modified herein, the Grievance Procedure shall be governed by Personnel Rule XV,
Disciplinary Proceedings, Sec. 6, Grievances, which is outlined as follows:

The presentation and hearing of all employee grievances shall be governed by the following rules:

A.  A grievance shall be defined as an alleged violation of a specific provision of this
  Memorandum of Understanding, the City Personnel Rules and Regulations, or ofthe Rules
  and Regulations validly propagated by any department within the City, or State Law
  governing conditions of employment. The grievance procedure shall not be utilized by an
  employee to contest the content of a performance evaluation, verbal or written reprimands,
  or other documentation regarding the employee's work perfoflnance, which is not defined
  as "disciplinary action" by Rule XV of the City Personnel Rules and Regulations.

  Discipline shall be imposed in such a manner as to not violate the FLSA with regard to
  "exempt" employees.

B  All grievances shall be filed in writing with the immediate supervisor of the person
  aggrieved within fifteen (15) calendar days after the employee knows, or in the exercise of
  reasonable diligence, would have known, of the occuffence in question.

C  Written notice of disposition of the grievance shall be filed with the next higher
  administrative authority by the supervisor with whom the grievance was originally frled.
  Such notice shall be filed within fifteen (15) calendar days of the original filing of the
  grievance.

D  If satisfactory redress is not obtained by the employee from the immediate supervisor, the
  grievance may be appealed in writing through the normal administrative organization: that
  is, first to the Division Manager; second, the Department Director and third, the City
  Manager. In each case, a written notice of disposition must be forwarded to the grievant
  and to the next higher authority within fifteen (15) calendar days of receipt of the
  employee's written grievance.

E.  The City Manager shall be the final authority in all cases except those in which a violation
  of the Personnel Ordinance or Rules is alleged. The City Manager shall forward notice of
  disposition of such grievance to the grievant within fifteen (15) calendar days of receipt of
  the employee's written grievance.

  ARTICLE 30: UNIT DETERMINATION AND MODIFICATION

A.  Policy and Standards for Determination of Appropriate Units

  The policy objectives in determining the appropriateness of units shall include: (1)
  efficient operations of the City and its compatibility with the primary responsibility of the
  City and its employees to effectively and economically serve the public, and on (2)
  providing employees with effective representation based on recognized community of
  interest considerations. These policy objectives require that the appropriate unit shall be
  the broadest feasible grouping ofpositions that share an identifiable community of interest.
  Factors to be considered shall be:

  1  Similarity of the general kinds of work performed, types of qualifications required,
  and the general working conditions.

  2.  History of representation in the City and in similar employment; except however,
  that no unit shall be deemed to be an appropriate unit solely on the basis of the
  extent to which employees in the proposed unit have organized.

  3.  Consistency with the organizational patterns of the City.

  4  Number of employees and classifications, and the effect on the administration of
  employer-employee relations because of the fragmentation of classifications andlor
  proliferation of units.

  5  Effect on the classification strucfure and impact on the stability of the ernployer-
  employee relationship because of dividing a single or related classification among
  two or more units.

  Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions of this Section, managerial, supervisory and
  confidential responsibilities, as defined in this Section, are determinative factors in
  establishing appropriate units hereunder. Therefore, such managerial, supervisory and
  confidential employees may not represent any employee organization that represents other
  employees and may not be represented by the same.

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Approving the license agreement between the City of Monterey Park and the
  Boys & Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Due to the ongoing pandemic, the Boys & Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley has
struggled to find parking to store their transportation vehicles. Staff has worked to assist
and has identified 12 parking spaces within the public parking lot graphically identified in
Exhibit "A" to the attached license to accommodate its vehicles.

BACKGROUND:

The Boys & Girls Club of West San Gabriel Valley has numerous transportation vehicles
that are used daily during normal operationaltimes. Due to the ongoing pandemic many
of those vehicles are not in use. The Boys & Girls Club struggled to find parking for those
vehicles during this time. The City identified 12 parking spaces for the temporary use by
the Boys & Girls Club, while the City's library is only offering limited services. The City
will license the Boys & Girls Club to use, on the terms and conditions in the attached
License, the 12 parking spaces identified within the public parking lot graphically identified
in Exhibit "A." This is a license to enter the library parking lot solely to accommodate the
Boys & Girls Club during the Emergency identified in Ordinance No. 2185 (adopted
August 5,2020) and in accordance with BRP2Parking.O10 of the 2020 Monterey Park
Business Recovery Program (the "Parking Program").

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a public works contract, in a form
  approved by the City Attorney, with GRBCON, lnc., in the amount of
  $2,393,089.00 for the N. Atlantic Sewer lmprovements, Specification No. 2020-07;
  2. Authorizing the appropriation of $881,926 from Sewer Funds and $300,000 from
  Measure R Funds for the construction of the project;
  3. Authorizing the lnterim Director of Public Works to approve change orders and
  contingency up to $359,000 (15%) of the contract amount, for a total project cost
  of $2,752,089; and
  4. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

GEQA (California Environmental Qualitv Act):
The proposed project is categorically exempt from the requirements of the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEOA) pursuant lo 14 California Code of Regulations $
15301 as a Class 1 categorical exemption (Existing Facilities). The Project results in
minor alterations to existing public facilities involving no significant expansion of the
existing use. The Project is not anticipated to have any significant impacts with regard to
traffic, noise, air quality or water quality.

W:
On September 2, 2020, the City Council rejected all bids received for the N. Atlantic
Water & Sewer lmprovement project Spec 2020-002 and authorized the re-advertisement
of the project as two separate projects. Staff completed the solicitation of bids for only the
sewer portion of the work. The deadline for the submittal of bids was December 1, 2020.
Staff completed the review of the bids and recommends the contract be awarded to
GRBCON, lnc. in the amount of $2,393,089; a 15% contingency is also requested for a
total project cost of $2,752,089.

W.S&.UND:
On June 20,2018, the City Council awarded a professional services agreement to SA
Associates to prepare plans, specifications, and estimates for the N. Atlantic Blvd. Water
and Sewer lmprovements project. lmprovements were planned to include replacement of

the water and sewer mains, primarily along N. Atlantic Blvd., from north of Newmark
Avenue to Hellman Avenue. During the design of the project, it was determined that
additional sewer improvements were necessary along Garvey Ave, from Atlantic Blvd. to
Ynez Ave. Final design included 2,450 feet of 12-in sewer main, 670 feet of 16-in sewer
main, and 900 feet of 18-in sewer main along N. Atlantic Blvd. and Garvey Avenue.

On August 6, 2020 bids were received for the N. Atlantic Water & Sewer lmprovement
Project (Bid Spec 2020-02). Based upon the bid prices - which resulted from various
specialization needed to do both projects - staff recommended to the City Council that
the project be divided into two separate projects. On September 2, 2020, the City Council
rejected all bids and approved staff's recommendation to separate the combined project
into two individual projects. Staff proceeded with the sewer project first to increase the
needed sewer capacity along Atlantic Blvd. and Garvey Ave. The improvements required
to increase sewer capacity along Garvey Ave. add significant costs to the project and are
planned to be funded from existing carryover sewer capital project funds.

Staff opened bids on December 1, 2020 on the N. Atlantic Sewer lmprovements Project,
Spec 2020-007, and has completed the review of all bids submitted. The bids are listed in

improvement project leaving available project budget of $844,211. ln addition, a total of
$725,952 available carryover Sewer Funds from various sewer projects will be utilized to

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Accepting the San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District (SGVMWD) 2020 Loan
  Program and authorizing the City Manager to execute an agreement, in a form
  approved by the City Attorney, with SGVMWD for a loan amount not to exceed
  $5M; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXEGUTIVE SUMMARY:
At its August 2020 meeting, the San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District (SGVMWD)
Board approved the 2020 Loan Program to assist member cities during the coronavirus
pandemic. lnterested cities are asked to submit requests not later than December 31,
2020.

With the passage of Assembly Bill 756, public water systems are now required to
monitor for polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in both drinking and groundwater. lf the
detection level in the treated water exceeds the maximum standard, the water system
must take the water source out of production.

ln response to the new mandate, the State Water Resource Board Division of Drinking
Water (DDW) is requiring the City of Monterey Park to include a PFAS removal system
as part of the Centralized Groundwater Treatment System (CGTS). City staff is currently
evaluating the various options for PFAS removal that would be acceptable to DDW. The
cost to design and build this additional system is estimated to be between $6 and $8
million.

BAGKGROUND:
Centralized Grou ndwater Treatment System
City Council awarded a design-build contract to J.R. Filanc Construction Company, lnc.
on August 17, 2016 to construct the Centralized Groundwater Treatment System

  Page 201 of 322
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 3
December 16,2020

(CGTS) at Delta Plant. Grant funds from the Prop 84 lntegrated Regional Water
Management program paid for half of the total project cost of $8.3M. The CGTS
upgrades the City's current treatment system that is aging and outdated with state-of-
the-art technology advanced oxidation/ultra-violet (AO/UV) reactors. The new
equipment can more effectively treat contaminants and remove a challenging toxic
chemical - 1,4 dioxane - that has been detected in the groundwater but cannot be
removed by the city's current system.

Assembly Bill 756 - California Health and Safety Code 5116378
ln the fall of 2018, the J.R. Filanc Project Team reached substantial completion of the
CGTS and began performance testing to obtain an operating permit from the State
Water Resource Board Division of Drinking Water (DDW). The process was stalled in
fall of 2019 when the State adopted California Health and Safety Code 5116378
(Assembly Bill 756) to address polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in public water
systems. PFAS chemicals have been used since the 1940s to water- and stain-proof
carpets, clothing, and other fabrics. lt is also used in cookware to create a non-stick
surface as well as for fire-retarding processes. Studies find that these chemicals have
adverse effects on the environment and are likely to be carcinogenic.

With the passage of 48756 and the detection of PFAS in the City's groundwater, DDW
informed the Project Team that a permit for the CGTS would not be granted until a
system for the removal of PFAS is constructed. The City's detection level has been as
high as 30 parts per trillion (ppt) as sampled at the water well, prior to treatment;
however, PFAS has not been detected in the City's treated water. PFAS concentration
that exceeds 70 ppt in potable water would require the water system to be taken offline.
The City's current water treatment system is able to remove PFAS through Granular
Activated Carbon (GAC) equipment and as such, DDW is allowing the City to continue
operations until the new system can be built.

Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) Removal Technology
ln August 2020, the City commissioned Trussell Technologies to begin conducting
Rapid SmallSca/e Colum lesfs (RSSCT) to determine which method of PFAS removal
would work best for Monterey Park's water treatment system. The two options for
removal are lon Exchange and GAC: The lon exchange method uses a resin to remove
PFAS, while GAC uses carbon to remove PFAS.

DDW has indicated a preference for lon exchange however this method can be more
costly. GAC can be just as effective depending upon the type of carbon used. Trussell is
expected to complete its analysis early next year. Once completed, the Filanc Project
Team can finalize its cost proposal for the new treatment system. Their initial cost
estimate is $6M for the GAC removal system and $8M for the lon Exchange system.

Due to the challenges of the coronavirus pandemic, the Board of the San Gabriel Valley
Municipal Water District (SGVMWD) approved the 2020 Loan Program for its member
cities. The zero-interest loan is to be funded by the District's financial reserves and will
have a term of no more than ten (10) years. Qualifying projects include infrastructure
replacement and treatment. SGVMWD determined that the City's proposed
PFOA/PFOS removal system is an eligible project.

The total budget for the 2020 Loan Program is $8M with $2M allocated to each of the
four member cities - Alhambra, Azusa, Monterey Park and Sierra Madre. At this time,
only the City of Sierra Madre expressed an interest in the loan, potentially leaving a
larger share to Monterey Park. Staff is requesting a loan of up to $5M depending on the
funds available. SGVMWD is requesting funding requests no later than December 31,
2020.

The SGVMWD loan is interest free to be paid over ten years. Should the City receive
the full amount of $5M, the annual payment is $500,000 for ten years. The funds to
repay the loan will be the City's water treatment fund (402).

an expenditure plan containing the following elements is submitted, reviewed and deemed
satisfactory by LACMTA. LACMTA staff will request that an expenditure plan be submitted
before making a recommendation to the LACMTA Board to program funds to that project:

o The estimated total cost for each project and program and/or each project or program
  activity;
o Funds other than Measure R that the project or program sponsor anticipates will be
  expended on the projects and programs and/or each project or program activity;
o The schedule during which the project sponsor anticipates funds will be available for
  each project and program andfor each project or program activity; and,

PROIECTTITLE:
Garfield Avenue Capacity Improvements [Hellman to Hilliard]

PROIECT LOCATTON:
The project is located in the northeastern portion of the City of Monterey Park on Garfield Avenue
just south of the Interstate 10 freeway eastbound on- and off-ramps.

PROIECT LIMITS:
The project limits are on Garfield Avenue from Hellman Avenue to Hilliard Avenue

NEXUS TO HTGHWAY OPERATTON, DEFINITION/PROIECT PURPOSE:
The proposed project involves the widening of Garfield Avenue between Hellman Avenue and
Hilliard Avenue. The improvements include additional lanes (a southbound lane and a center two-
way left-turn lane) to increase capacity, improve tra{Iic flow, and reduce congestion along Garfield
Avenue, which will continue to worsen over time without improvements.

PROJECT BACKGROUND:
The proposed prol'ect was identified, and was awarded LACMTA Measure R funding, as part of a
broader package of projects known as the SR-710 Mobility Improvement Projects (MIPs). The SR-710
MIPs are the result of reallocated Measure R Funds for the SR-710 North Project to new mobility
improvement projects within the San Gabriel Valley subregion. These projects are consistent with
the purpose and need of the Gap Closure Project to relieve congestion on local streets along the SR-
710 alignment between Interstates 10 (I-10) and 210 (I-210), with the highest priority for projects
proximate to the I-10 freeway. Garfield Avenue is a north-south regional corridor and provides access
to communities befiveen State Route 60 to the south and I-210 freeway to the north. Garfield Avenue
provides access to and from the I-10 freeway. The addition of a third southbound lane will increase
roadway capacity and improve trafhc flow, especially for the southbound traffic exiting the I-10
freeway.

SCOPE:
The City plans to widen Garfield Avenue with an additional southbound lane and a center two-way
left-turn lane between Hellman Avenue and Hilliard Avenue. The existing street has two lanes in
each direction. The project includes roadway rehabilitation, changing the striping alignment to
accommodate the new lanes, landscaping (e.g., street trees), and relocation of the monument sign.
The additional lanes can be accommodated within the existing Right-ofWay (ROW) however, on-
street parking will be prohibited. The length of the project is approximately 1,000 feet.

PROJECTTITLE:
Atlantic Blvd Capacity Improvements [Hellman to Garvey]

PROIECT LOCATTON:
The project is located in the northeastern portion of the City of Monterey Park on Atlantic Boulevard
south of the Interstate 10 freeway on- and offramps.

PROIECT LIMITS:
The project limits include Atlantic Boulevard from Hellman Avenue to Garvey Avenue.

NEXUS TO HTGHWAY OPERATION, DEFINITION/PROJECT PURPOSE:
The Project contributes to mobility and operational benefits in the SR-710 corridor between I-10 and
I-210 consistent with the Purpose and Need of the 710 Gap Closure project. The proposed project
involves improvements to Atlantic Boulevard from Hellman Avenue to Garvey Avenue. The
improvements include additional lanes to increase capacity, improve tra{fic flow, and reduce
congestion along Atlantic Boulevard, which will continue to worsen over time without
improvements.

PROJECT BACKGROUND:
The proposed project was identified, and was awarded LACMTA Measure R funding, as part of a
broader package of projects known as the SR-710 Mobility Improvement Projects (MIPs). The SR-710
MIPs are the result of reallocated Measure R Funds for the SR-710 North Project to new mobility
improvement projects within the San Gabriel Valley subregion. These projects are consistent with
the purpose and need of the Gap Closure Project to relieve congestion on local streets along the SR-
710 alignment between Interstates 10 (I-10) and 21.0 (I-210), with the highest priority for projects
proximate to the Interstate 10 freeway. Atlantic Boulevard is a north-south regional corridor that
provides access to communities between the State Route 60 freeway to the south and the I-210
freeway to the north. Atlantic Boulevard provides access to and from the I-10 freeway. The addition of
a southbound lane on Atlantic Boulevard will increase the capacity and improve traflic flow,
particularly for southbound travel coming from the I-10 Freeway.

  SCOPE OF WORK

PROIECTTITLE:
Ramona Road Capacity Improvements [710 Off-Ramp s/o I-10 Freeway]

PROIECT LOCATTON:
The project is located in the City of Monterey Park at Ramona Road/710 ofFramp south of I-10
Freeway.

PROJECT LIMITS:
The project limits are Ramona Road off-ramp on I-710 northbound (located south of I-10 Freeway) to
Corporate Center Drive, and Corporate Center Drive from the I-710 off-ramp to approximately 300
feet south of the I-710 off-ramp.

NEXUS TO HTGHWAY OPERATION, DEFINITION/PROfECT PURPOSE:
The Project contributes to mobility and operational benefits in the SR-710 corridor between I-10 and
I-210 consistent with the Purpose and Need of the 710 Gap Closure project. The proposed project
involves improvements to Ramona Road/710 off-ramp south of I-10 Freeway. The improvements
include an additional lane on the off-ramp to increase capacity, improve traflic flow, and reduce
congestion at this location, which will continue to worsen over time without improvements.

PROJECT BACKGROUND:
The proposed project was identified, and was awarded LACMTA Measure R funding, as part of a
broader package of projects known as the SR-710 Mobility Improvement Projects (MIPs). The SR-710
MIPs are the result of reallocated Measure R Funds for the SR-710 North Project to new mobility

SUBJECT:  City's use of Community Development Block Grants (CDBG) funds to
  mitigate the adverse financial impact of the LA County Health Directive
  prohibiting outdoor and indoor dining to Monterey Park Restaurants.

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing a report from the City Manager regarding the City's use of
  CDBG funds to reimburse the restaurants of Monterey Park for the costs of their
  food delivery service for a period of 31 days to mitigate the adverse financial
  impact of the LA County Health Directive prohibiting outdoor and indoor dining.
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On Saturday, December 5, 2020, the Los Angeles County Health Department issued a
new County Health Order to suspend outdoor and indoor dining at restaurants for at
least three weeks starting Sunday, December 6th amid the County's worst coronavirus
spike yet. Restaurants are only able to offer take-out, drive thru, and delivery services.

This directive has had a devastating effect on our City's battered restaurant industry and
will cripple so many livelihoods, risking permanently losing businesses, jobs, and
community assets. The restaurants that can survive, mostly through layoffs and
furloughs, fear their businesses will be insolvent without federal assistance that seems
unlikely to come. The threat is only magnified by the Holiday season. Restaurant
owners say they often make up for down months during the Holidays.

Following staff's analysis of the devastating effect this Health directive will have on our
City's battered restaurant industry, staff has determined that it is in the City's best
interest to provide financial assistance to our City's restaurant by using Community
Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds to subsidize restaurant food delivery cost.

As our City's restaurants suffer through more restrictions forced by the pandemic, we
must focus on both short-term and long{erm solutions to help them survive. We need

  Page 315 of 322

Page 2 of 4

new, alternative business assistance models that are innovative, inclusive, and
equitable - we must rebuild better and a new City program called Restaurant Delivery
Assistance Program funded by CDBG is a good start.

BACKGROUND:

A food delivery service allows restaurants to maintain safety and provide much needed
income, especially during the outdoor dining ban. More important, online food delivery
companies offer restaurants a new way to make money, reach new diners, and deliver
food to their customers.

Restaurants that use online food delivery companies pay an additional commission on
the transaction for use of those services. An online delivery service company like Uber
Eats charges a restaurant around 3oo/o of their listed prices for the privilege of delivering
their food. For example, ABC Restaurant charges $30 for a lunch order, Uber Eats
would take around $9 dollars as a fee for delivering their food.

The problem here is that the average profit margin for a restaurant is under 30%. Fast
foods such as McDonalds reported profit margins about 22o/o in 2018. According to the
California Restaurant Association, casual dining or family style restaurants have a profit
margin of 5oh lo 10%. And full-service restaurants such as fine-dining have average
profit margins of about 6.1o/o.

Based on the average profit margins above, every restaurant that engages Uber Eats
will lose money on every order they take. The more orders coming from Uber Eats, the
more money a restaurant would lose. Thus, many of our small restaurants in Monterey
Park are hesitant to sign-up with online delivery companies due to the high cost. For
example, out of Monterey Park's 207 restaurants, only 43 are signed up with DoorDash
and 60 are signed up with Fantuan Delivery, a delivery company specializing in the
Asian market.

To be fair, food delivery service companies like Uber Eats do bring something to the
table, like literally thousands of new customers. Through online apps, they provide
marketing access to a whole new audience and give restaurants the power to deliver
directly to customers, with no investment, infrastructure, or logistical nightmares.

To mitigate the devastating effect of the ban on outdoor dining to our restaurants, the
City of Monterey Park will use CDBG funds to subsidize restaurant delivery costs, with a
maximum subsidy amount per restaurant of $1,000. The program begins on Monday,
December 14, 2020 and run for 31 days through January 15, 2021. This program will
not only allow restaurants to maintain safety while generating much needed revenue, it
will also create more dining options for our residents by encouraging more restaurants
that had never considered food delivery service to be a viable option to finally adopt the
service and technology.

  Page 316 of 322

Page 3 of 4

Additionally, City staff has negotiated a special discounted pricing structure with three
food service delivery companies, namely DoorDash, Chowbus, and Fantuan Delivery,
for all restaurants participating in the program. These special pricing discounts on
delivery fees and commissions range from 20o/o to 90% reduction from standard rates
that these companies normally charge. Not only will these heavily discounted rates help
our existing restaurant users of delivery service generate more much needed revenue, it
will also encourage and attract restaurants that are non-users within our community to
sign up for delivery service and create new sources of revenue.

To fund the Restaurant Delivery Service Program, $120,000 dollars of the total CDBG
funds previously approved by Council for the Small Business Assistance Program
(SBAP) will be shifted toward the program. The City of Monterey Park has 207
restaurants, of which 152 are classified as full-service (20-seat capacity and above) and
55 eateries (smaller restaurants, bakeries, tea/boba shops, pizzerias, etc.). Due to the
limited funds, the program will reimburse up to $1,000 of delivery service fees to
participating restaurants and will be made available to the first 120 restaurants enrolled
on a first-come, first-served basis. However, the more restaurants we can direct toward
signing up with our three preferred service providers with their much lower rates, the
more restaurants we can allow to participate in the program. National brands like IHOP,
Marie Callenders, and other franchised restaurants will be excluded from this program,
as they already have existing preferred rates with delivery service companies obtained
through their national franchises.

FISCAL IMPAGT:

There are no direct foreseeable costs to the City with the restaurant delivery fee
subsidy. lt is anticipated that the CDBG fund will pay for the entire subsidy.

  minimum wage increase will impact ten (10) positions that are below the mandated
  increase as follows: Cashier, Junior Lifeguard, Library Page, Locker Room

  TREATMENT OF PERFLUOROOCTANOIC ACID (PFAS)

  At its August 2020 meeting, the San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water District
  (SGVMWD) Board approved the 2020 Loan Program to assist member cities
  during the coronavirus pandemic. Interested cities are asked to submit requests
  not later than December 31, 2020.

  With the passage of Assembly Bill 756, public water systems are now required to
  monitor for polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in both drinking and groundwater. If
   68-312
  December 16, 2020
  the detection level in the treated water exceeds the maximum standard, the water
  system must take the water source out of production.

  In response to the new mandate, the State Water Resource Board Division of
  Drinking Water (DDW) is requiring the City of Monterey Park to include a PFAS
  removal system as part of the Centralized Groundwater Treatment System
  (CGTS). City staff is currently evaluating the various options for PFAS removal that
  would be acceptable to DDW. The cost to design and build this additional system
  is estimated to be between $6 and $8 million.

  Action Taken: The City Council accepted the San Gabriel Valley Municipal Water

5B. CITY’S USE OF COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT BLOCK GRANTS (CDBG)
  FUNDS TO MITIGATE THE ADVERSE FINANCIAL IMPACT OF THE LA
  COUNTY HEALTH DIRECTIVE PROHIBITING OUTDOOR AND INDOOR
  DINING TO MONTEREY PARK RESTAURANTS

  On December 5, 2020, the Los Angeles County Health Department issued a new
  County Health Order to suspend outdoor and indoor dining at restaurants for at
  least three weeks starting Sunday, December 6th amid the County’s worst
  coronavirus spike yet. Restaurants are only able to offer take-out, drive thru, and
  delivery services.

  This directive has had a devastating effect on our City’s battered restaurant
  industry and will cripple so many livelihoods, risking permanently losing
  businesses, jobs, and community assets. The restaurants that can survive, mostly
  through layoffs and furloughs, fear their businesses will be insolvent without federal
  assistance that seems unlikely to come. The threat is only magnified by the
  Holiday season. Restaurant owners say they often make up for down months
  during the Holidays.

  Following staff’s analysis of the devastating effect this Health directive will have on
  our City’s battered restaurant industry, staff has determined that it is in the City’s
  best interest to provide financial assistance to our City’s restaurant by using
  Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds to subsidize restaurant food
  delivery cost.

  As our City’s restaurants suffer through more restrictions forced by the pandemic,
  we must focus on both short-term and long-term solutions to help them survive.
  We need new, alternative business assistance models that are innovative,
  inclusive, and equitable – we must rebuild better and a new City program called
  Restaurant Delivery Assistance Program funded by CDBG is a good start.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed a report from the City Manager
  regarding the City’s use of CDBG funds to reimburse the restaurants of Monterey
  Park for the costs of their food delivery service for a period of 31 days to mitigate
  the adverse financial impact of the LA County Health Directive prohibiting outdoor
  and indoor dining.
